questions.q: What is a landform?
questions.a: A physical feature on the surface of the Earth
o: A physical feature on the surface of the Earth
Water from the atmosphere reaching the ground
The height of an object above sea level
A type of forest that grows on mountain slopes

questions.q: By which set of features can a mountain be recognised?
questions.a: A broad base, steep slopes and a narrow summit
o: A broad base, steep slopes and a narrow summit
A raised surface that is more or less flat on top
A flat or gently undulating surface with no deep valleys
A lower height, less steep slopes and a rounded top

questions.q: A mountain has a broad base, steep slopes and a narrow summit. A geographer is shown a highland and may check only ONE feature to decide whether it is a plateau or a mountain. Which feature should she check?
questions.a: Whether its top is flat or comes to a narrow summit
o: Whether its top is flat or comes to a narrow summit
Whether it stands several hundred metres above sea level
Whether some of its sides are steep slopes
Whether it is rich in deposits of minerals

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Hills are lower in height than mountains.
Reason (R): Hills have steeper slopes than mountains.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: State True or False, and give a reason: 'Snow and hailstones are both forms of precipitation.'
questions.a: True. Precipitation is water from the atmosphere reaching the ground in any form; snow and hailstones are precipitation of water in a solid state.
s: States the verdict: True
Explains that precipitation is water reaching the ground in any form, and snow and hail are water in a solid state

questions.q: (a) What is meant by 'altitude'? (b) Give one example of altitude from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Altitude is the height of an object above sea level. (b) For example, the altitude of a mountain (also accept the altitude of a bird or plane in flight, or of a satellite).
s: Defines altitude as the height of an object above sea level
Gives one example: a mountain, a bird or plane in flight, or a satellite

questions.q: A school on a plain and a school high in a snowy mountain region exchange letters about the land around them. (a) Write one feature of the land around the mountain school that the plain school would not see. (b) The mountain school writes that its stream runs full every summer even in weeks with no rain. Using the chapter, explain why.
questions.a: (a) Mountains that rise much higher than the land around them, with steep slopes and narrow summits (or snow-capped peaks). (b) At lower altitudes the snow on the mountains melts every summer and turns into water that feeds the rivers and streams.
s: Names a mountain feature: steep slopes, a narrow summit or snow-capped peaks rising far above the land around
Explains that snow melts every summer and the water feeds the stream

questions.q: (a) Name the three categories into which landforms are broadly divided. (b) The chapter says humans have adapted to all landforms. What does it say about the number of people living on different kinds of landforms? (c) What are highlands with a lower height, less steep slopes and rounded tops called?
questions.a: (a) Mountains, plateaus and plains. (b) The number of people living on different kinds of landforms varies throughout the world. (c) Hills.
s: Names mountains, plateaus and plains
States that the number of people varies from one kind of landform to another
Names them as hills

questions.q: Kiran says: 'Every mountain is covered with snow throughout the year.' Test Kiran's claim using the chapter, giving three points.
questions.a: Kiran's claim is wrong. (1) Whether a mountain has snow depends on its height: the chapter says only some mountains are covered with snow. (2) At lower altitudes the snow melts every summer and turns into water that feeds rivers, so those mountains are not snow-covered all year. (3) Only at high altitudes may the snow never melt, so only those mountains are permanently snow-capped.
s: States that snow cover depends on the mountain's height, so only some mountains have snow
Explains that at lower altitudes the snow melts every summer and feeds rivers
Explains that only at high altitudes the snow may never melt, giving permanently snow-capped peaks, so the claim is wrong

questions.q:
Name the landform described in each line, using the chapter.
(a) A range of tall, sharp peaks whose lower slopes are covered with pine and deodar forest.
(b) Land that rises from the country around it to about 1,000 m and is more or less flat on top, with a steep slope on one side.
(c) A wide, flat stretch about 100 m above sea level, where a river from the mountains has laid down silt.
(d) A highland lower than the mountains near it, with gentle slopes and a rounded top.
(e) A large, dry expanse that gets very little precipitation in a year.
questions.a: (a) Mountains (a young mountain range). (b) A plateau. (c) A plain (a floodplain). (d) A hill. (e) A desert.
s: (a) Mountains
(b) Plateau
(c) Plain or floodplain
(d) Hill
(e) Desert

questions.q: Which mountain range does the chapter place in South America?
questions.a: The Andes

questions.q: Which feature shows that a mountain range is relatively 'young'?
questions.a: Tall and sharp peaks

questions.q:
Match each mountain in Column A with its location in Column B.
Column A: 1. Mount Everest  2. Kanchenjunga  3. Mount Kilimanjaro  4. Anamudi
Column B: A. Kerala, in south India  B. between Tibet (China) and Nepal  C. eastern Africa  D. between Nepal and Sikkim

Read the statements about the montane forest.
I. Its conifer trees have broad, flat leaves.
II. At higher altitudes, its trees give way to grasses, mosses and lichen.
III. Pines, firs, spruce and deodar are common in it.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only

questions.q: (a) How are most of the world's mountains arranged, according to the chapter? (b) Give one example of this, naming the continent in which it lies.
questions.a: (a) Most of the world's mountains are grouped in mountain ranges, some stretching for thousands of kilometres. (b) The Himalayas in Asia (also accept the Alps in Europe or the Andes in South America).
s: States that most mountains are grouped in mountain ranges
Names one range with its continent: Himalayas-Asia, Alps-Europe or Andes-South America

questions.q: (a) Ankit says: 'The Aravalli Range is shorter than the Himalayas, so it must be the younger range.' Correct Ankit using the chapter. (b) What has given the Aravalli Range its rounded shape?
questions.a: (a) It is the other way round: the shorter, rounded Aravalli Range is much older, while the tall, sharp Himalayas are relatively young. (b) Erosion, over a very long time, has rounded the Aravallis.
s: States that the Aravallis are older and the Himalayas are the young range
Names erosion as what rounded the Aravallis

questions.q: (a) Name two birds that the chapter lists among the fauna of the mountains. (b) Name two other mountain animals from the same list that are not birds.
questions.a: (a) The golden eagle and the peregrine falcon. (b) Any two of: the Canadian lynx, snow leopard, ibex, Himalayan tahr, mountain hare, yak, grey fox and black bear.
s: Names the golden eagle and the peregrine falcon
Names two non-bird animals from the list, such as the snow leopard and the yak

questions.q: (a) Which peak is the highest of the Andes? (b) Which is the highest mountain of the Alps, and in which part of Europe is it? (c) Which is the highest mountain in south India, and what is its other name?
questions.a: (a) Mount Aconcagua. (b) Mont Blanc, in Western Europe. (c) Anamudi in Kerala, also known as 'Anai Peak'.
s: Names Mount Aconcagua
Names Mont Blanc and Western Europe
Names Anamudi and its other name, Anai Peak

questions.q: Sana says: 'The Himalayas were formed millions of years ago, so they are old mountains that have stopped changing.' Test Sana's claim, giving three points from the chapter.
questions.a: Sana's claim is wrong. (1) The Himalayas are called relatively 'young' because they formed recently in the Earth's history, even though that is still millions of years ago; 'young' is measured against the Earth's history. (2) Their tall, sharp peaks mark them as young, unlike the much older Aravalli Range, which erosion has rounded. (3) In the Himalayas, upliftment as well as erosion continue to this day, and they are still growing in height, so they have not stopped changing.
s: Explains that 'young' is measured against the Earth's history, so millions of years ago is still recent
Uses the tall, sharp peaks (against the old, rounded Aravallis) as the sign of a young range
States that upliftment and erosion continue and the Himalayas are still growing, so they have not stopped changing

questions.q: Justify the statement: 'Not all mountains are alike.' Use five different points from the chapter, about (i) whether they belong to a range, (ii) their age and shape, (iii) their height, (iv) their snow cover and (v) where in the world they stand.
questions.a: (i) Most mountains are grouped in ranges such as the Himalayas, Alps and Andes, but Mount Kilimanjaro in eastern Africa is an isolated mountain that is not part of any range. (ii) Young mountains like the Himalayas have tall, sharp peaks, while old ones like the Aravalli Range are shorter and rounded by erosion. (iii) Heights differ greatly: Mount Everest, at 8,848 m, is the highest in the world, while Anamudi is the highest only in south India. (iv) Depending on height, some mountains are permanently snow-capped, while on lower ones the snow melts every summer. (v) They stand on different continents: Everest and Kanchenjunga in Asia, Aconcagua in South America, Mont Blanc in Western Europe, Kilimanjaro in eastern Africa. So mountains differ in many ways, which justifies the statement.
s: Ranges against an isolated mountain: Kilimanjaro is not part of any range
Young, sharp Himalayas against old, rounded Aravallis worn by erosion
Height differs: Everest 8,848 m and highest in the world, Anamudi highest only in south India
Snow cover depends on height: some permanently snow-capped, others lose their snow each summer
Different continents, with at least three correct examples

questions.q: Followers of Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Bon all hold one mountain in Tibet sacred. Which mountain is it?
questions.a: Mount Kailash

questions.q: On steep mountain slopes, farmers grow crops by cutting steps into the slope. What is this way of farming called?
questions.a: Terrace farming

questions.q: The chapter says Arunima Sinha 'went on to climb the highest peak of every continent, including Mount Vinson in Antarctica'. What can you conclude about Mount Vinson from this line?
questions.a: It is the highest peak of Antarctica
o: It is the highest peak of Antarctica
It is the highest peak of the Himalayas
It is an isolated peak in eastern Africa
It is the highest mountain of the Alps

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Tourism is often an important source of income for people living in the mountains.
Reason (R): The crisp mountain air and scenic beauty attract many tourists.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each mountain hazard in Column A with its meaning in Column B.
Column A: 1. Avalanche  2. Landslide  3. Flash flood  4. Cloudburst
Column B: A. a sudden, violent rainstorm  B. a sudden local flood  C. the sudden collapse of a mass of earth or rock from a mountainside  D. the sudden fall of snow, ice or rocks from a mountainside

(a) Bachendri Pal was awarded the Padma Shri in 1984 and the Padma Bhushan in 2019. How many years apart were the two awards? (b) Arunima Sinha climbed Mount Everest in 2013 and was awarded the Padma Shri in 2015. How many years after her climb did she receive it?
s: Finds 2019 - 1984 = 35 years
Finds 2015 - 2013 = 2 years

questions.q: (a) Give two reasons from the chapter why people travel to the mountains. (b) The chapter says it is 'often difficult to find the right balance' in mountain tourism. Between which two things must the balance be found?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: the crisp mountain air and scenic beauty; sports such as skiing, hiking, mountaineering and paragliding; pilgrimages to holy sites. (b) Between the income that tourism brings to mountain people and protecting the fragile mountain environment, which an excessive inflow of visitors puts under pressure.
s: Gives two reasons: air and scenery, sports, or pilgrimage
Names the balance: tourism income against the pressure of too many visitors on the fragile environment

questions.q: (a) A weather office warns of a cloudburst over a mountain valley. Which other hazard should villagers further down the valley prepare for, and why? (b) Name the hazard that the chapter says often occurs when the snow starts melting. (c) The chapter's pictures of mountain challenges include 'uncontrolled tourism' beside avalanches, landslides and cloudbursts. In what way is it different from the others?
questions.a: (a) A flash flood, because a flash flood is a sudden local flood that is often caused by a cloudburst. (b) An avalanche. (c) Uncontrolled tourism is a human-made challenge, while avalanches, landslides and cloudbursts are natural.
s: Names a flash flood and links it to the cloudburst as its frequent cause
Names the avalanche
States that uncontrolled tourism is human-made while the others are natural

questions.q:
A school in Dehradun sets up an exhibition on Mount Everest with four boards. Board 1 gives the mountain's height and shows a map of the border on which it stands. Board 2 shows a prayer flag carrying the name the Tibetans give the mountain. Board 3 shows the name the Nepalis use for it. Board 4 shows a woman climber who reached the top in 1984, the first Indian woman to do so.
(a) Between which two places does Mount Everest stand?
(b) What name would Board 2 show, and what does it mean?
(c) What name would Board 3 show, and what does it mean?
(d) Name the climber on Board 4, and the climber she encouraged and trained who climbed Everest in 2013.
questions.a: (a) Between Tibet (China) and Nepal. (b) 'Chomolungma', meaning 'Mother Goddess of the World'. (c) 'Sagarmatha', meaning 'Goddess of the Sky'. (d) Bachendri Pal; she encouraged and trained Arunima Sinha.
s: (a) Tibet (China) and Nepal
(b) Chomolungma, Mother Goddess of the World
(c) Sagarmatha, Goddess of the Sky
(d) Bachendri Pal and Arunima Sinha

questions.q: A mountain panchayat has money for only one project this year. Project P: buy 60 more sheep and goats for the village's herders. Project Q: build a trekking trail and a small rest-house to bring visitors for hiking and the views. (a) What about mountain land limits regular farming, and which occupation does the chapter say is often preferred in mountain regions? (b) Why could Project Q bring income, according to the chapter? (c) State one risk of Project Q that the chapter warns about. (d) Recommend one project and justify it, weighing both sides.
questions.a: (a) The terrain is rugged with steep slopes, so regular farming is possible only in some valleys; herding is often preferred over agriculture. (b) Tourism is often an important source of income in the mountains: the crisp air and scenic beauty attract tourists, and many come for sports such as hiking. (c) An excessive inflow of visitors can put the fragile mountain environment under pressure. (d) Either choice earns the mark if it is weighed: P builds on herding, the occupation the chapter says is preferred, and puts no pressure from visitors on the land; Q can bring new income but must limit visitor numbers to protect the environment.
s: Rugged, steep terrain limits farming to some valleys; herding is often preferred
Q brings tourist income because the air, scenery and sports such as hiking attract visitors
Risk: too many visitors put the fragile mountain environment under pressure
Recommends one project with a reason that weighs the other side

questions.q: Which plateau has been nicknamed the 'Roof of the World'?
questions.a: The Tibetan Plateau

questions.q: Huge reserves of which minerals are found in India's Chhota Nagpur Plateau?
questions.a: Iron, coal and manganese

questions.q:
Read the statements about waterfalls on plateaus.
I. The Jog Falls are on the Sharavati River in the Western Ghats.
II. The Hundru Falls are on the Sharavati River in the Chhota Nagpur Plateau.
III. The Nohkalikai Falls drop 340 metres from the Cherrapunji Plateau in Meghalaya.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Many plateaus are less favourable to farming than plains.
Reason (R): Plateaus are rich in mineral deposits.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: State True or False, and give a reason: 'All plateaus are young in terms of the Earth's history.'
questions.a: False. Like mountains, plateaus can be young or old in terms of the Earth's history; the Deccan Plateau, for example, is one of the oldest plateaus in the world.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: plateaus can be young or old, for example the Deccan Plateau is one of the oldest

questions.q: (a) What is a plateau? (b) Name one plateau in India that the chapter mentions.
questions.a: (a) A plateau is a landform that rises up from the surrounding land and has a more or less flat surface; some of its sides are often steep slopes. (b) The Deccan Plateau (also accept the Chhota Nagpur Plateau or the Cherrapunji Plateau).
s: Defines a plateau as land rising from its surroundings with a more or less flat surface
Names an Indian plateau: Deccan, Chhota Nagpur or Cherrapunji

questions.q: (a) Why have plateaus been called 'storehouses of minerals'? (b) Which plateau is famous for gold and diamond mining? (c) How much can the height of plateaus vary, according to the chapter?
questions.a: (a) Plateaus are rich in mineral deposits, so mining is a major activity on them and many of the world's largest mines are found there. (b) The East African Plateau. (c) From a few hundred metres to several thousand metres.
s: Explains that plateaus are rich in mineral deposits, with mining a major activity
Names the East African Plateau
States from a few hundred metres to several thousand metres

questions.q: A river crosses a raised, flat-topped upland and then drops over its steep edge as a waterfall. A survey team finds that the pool at the foot of the falls is 620 m above sea level and that the water drops 340 m. (a) Find the height of the top of the falls above sea level. (b) Could the flat land at the top be a plain? Give a reason from the chapter. (c) The chapter names a waterfall in Meghalaya with this same drop. Name it and the plateau it falls from.
questions.a: (a) 620 + 340 = 960 m above sea level. (b) No. Plains are generally not more than 300 m above sea level, and this land is raised above its surroundings with a flat top and a steep side, so it is a plateau. (c) The Nohkalikai Falls, which drop from the Cherrapunji Plateau.
s: Says it cannot be a plain, since plains are generally not more than 300 m and this raised, flat-topped land is a plateau
Names the Nohkalikai Falls and the Cherrapunji Plateau

questions.q:
A Class 6 group from Ranchi goes on a two-day field trip in the Chhota Nagpur region of Jharkhand. On Day 1 they visit a coal mine and an iron-ore mine, and the guide says the region also has large reserves of manganese. On Day 2 they meet a farmer whose two fields have thin, rocky soil; she says her harvest is small unless the rains are very good.
(a) Which landform is the Chhota Nagpur region? Give one feature from the chapter that marks this landform.
(b) Why does the chapter call such landforms 'storehouses of minerals'?
(c) Using the chapter, explain why the farmer's harvest is small.
(d) A classmate concludes: 'So no plateau in India can be good for farming.' Evaluate this conclusion.
questions.a: (a) A plateau: it rises up from the surrounding land and has a more or less flat surface. (b) Plateaus are rich in mineral deposits, so mining is a major activity on them and many of the world's largest mines are found there. (c) Many plateaus have a rocky soil, which makes them less fertile than plains and less favourable to farming. (d) The conclusion goes too far. Lava plateaus, formed through volcanic activity, often have a rich black soil; the Deccan Plateau was formed through volcanic activity, so parts of a plateau can be good for farming. Rocky soil is common but not true of every plateau.
s: (a) Plateau, with a feature such as land rising from its surroundings with a flat top
(b) Rich in mineral deposits, so mining is a major activity
(c) Rocky soil makes many plateaus less fertile and less favourable to farming
(d) Rejects the conclusion using lava plateaus and their rich black soil, with the volcanic Deccan as the Indian example

questions.q: Compare a plateau with a mountain under five heads, using the chapter: (a) the shape of the top, (b) the slopes or sides, (c) height, (d) age in the Earth's history, and (e) mineral wealth and the work it leads to. For each head, say whether the two are alike or different.
questions.a: (a) Different: a mountain has a narrow summit; a plateau has a more or less flat surface. (b) Partly alike: a mountain has a broad base and steep slopes; a plateau rises from the land around it and some of its sides are often steep slopes. (c) Different: a mountain is much higher than the land around it, while a plateau's height varies from a few hundred metres to several thousand metres (the Tibetan Plateau averages 4,500 m). (d) Alike: like mountains, plateaus can be young or old (young Himalayas, old Aravallis; the Deccan is one of the oldest plateaus). (e) Alike in wealth: like mountains, plateaus are rich in mineral deposits; on plateaus this makes mining a major activity, earning them the name 'storehouses of minerals'.
s: (a) Narrow summit against a more or less flat top: different
(b) Mountains have steep slopes; plateaus often have some steep sides: partly alike
(c) Mountains are much higher than their surroundings; plateau heights vary from a few hundred to several thousand metres
(d) Both can be young or old, with an example
(e) Both are rich in minerals; on plateaus mining is a major activity ('storehouses of minerals')

questions.q: What does the chapter mean by 'sediments'?
questions.a: Particles of rock, sand and silt that rivers carry
o: Particles of rock, sand and silt that rivers carry
Water that reaches the ground as rain, snow or hail
Steps cut into a slope so that crops can be grown
Minerals such as iron, coal and manganese

questions.q: Where did the first civilisations develop, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Around rivers in fertile plains
o: On high plateaus rich in minerals
At the edges of large hot deserts

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Agriculture in the Ganga plain has traditionally depended mostly on water from canals.
Reason (R): Irrigation has increased agricultural production in the Ganga plain.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q:
Read the statements about plains.
I. Plains are generally not more than 300 metres above sea level.
II. Because plains have a gentle slope, river navigation on them is easy.
III. About 40 lakh people live in India's Ganga plain.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only

questions.q: (a) What is a confluence? (b) Give one way in which confluences matter to people in India, according to the chapter.
questions.a: (a) A confluence is the meeting point of two or more rivers. (b) Many communities consider a river's confluence with other rivers sacred, and numerous festivals, ceremonies and rituals are held at such places.
s: Defines a confluence as the meeting point of two or more rivers
States that confluences are held sacred and festivals, ceremonies or rituals are held there

questions.q: A river begins high in a mountain range and flows down to a wide plain. (a) What does the river collect in the mountains, and what does it do with it in the plain? (b) How does this help farming in the plain?
questions.a: (a) It collects particles of rock, sand and silt (sediments), carries them to the plain and deposits them there. (b) The deposits make the soil very fertile, so the plain is ideal for growing crops of all kinds.
s: States that the river collects rock, sand and silt (sediments) and deposits them in the plain
Explains that the deposits make the soil very fertile, good for crops of all kinds

questions.q: (a) Name two food crops grown in the Ganga plain. (b) Name two fibre crops grown there. (c) Besides agriculture, name one major occupation of people in the Ganga plain.
questions.a: (a) Any two of rice, wheat, maize, barley and millets. (b) Any two of cotton, jute and hemp. (c) River fishing.
s: Names two food crops such as rice and wheat
Names two fibre crops from cotton, jute and hemp
Names river fishing

questions.q:
Sunita farms four fields in a village on the Ganga plain. Two fields, of rice and wheat, are watered only by rain, as her grandparents did. The other two, of jute and maize, get water from a pump that draws groundwater, and they give bigger harvests. Ten years ago the village pump reached water 8 m below the ground; now it must go down 14 m.
(a) Which of Sunita's four crops is a fibre crop?
(b) By how many metres has the water level fallen in ten years, and what does the chapter call this?
(c) Why do her pump-watered fields give bigger harvests, according to the chapter?
(d) Sunita plans to put all four fields on the pump. Should she? Give a justified judgement.
questions.a: (a) Jute (rice, wheat and maize are food crops). (b) 14 - 8 = 6 m; the chapter calls this the depletion (decrease) of groundwater. (c) Irrigation has increased agricultural production in the Ganga plain. (d) A judgement that weighs both sides: pumping all four fields would raise her harvests, but more pumping would speed up the fall in groundwater, already 6 m in ten years, which the chapter calls a challenge for the future of agriculture; so she should be careful, for example keeping some fields rainfed. A 'yes' that answers the groundwater risk also earns the mark.
s: (a) Jute
(b) 6 m, called depletion of groundwater
(c) Irrigation has increased agricultural production
(d) Decision that weighs bigger harvests against faster groundwater depletion

questions.q: A school on the Ganga plain is writing a booklet called 'Our river and us'. Using the chapter, write one short section on each of these four ways the river matters to people of the plain: (a) farming, (b) work other than farming, (c) moving from place to place, (d) culture and religion.
questions.a: (a) Farming: the river carries sediments from the mountains and deposits them, making the soil very fertile; its water is also brought to fields through canals. (b) Other work: river fishing is a major occupation, and river navigation supports a lot of economic activity. (c) Moving around: because plains have a gentle slope, river navigation is easy; people once travelled by river a great deal, and on some stretches of the Ganga people still prefer boats. (d) Culture: many communities consider a river's source and its confluence with other rivers sacred, and festivals, ceremonies and rituals are held there.
s: (a) Fertile sediment soil, and canal water, for farming
(b) River fishing, and navigation supporting economic activity
(c) Gentle slope makes navigation easy; boats still used on some stretches
(d) Sources and confluences held sacred, with festivals and rituals there

questions.q: Justify the statement: 'Plains have long been a favoured home for people, but life there is not free of problems.' Give four points that show why plains attract people and one point on their problems.
questions.a: (1) Plains are flat or gently undulating, and rivers deposit sediments on them that make the soil very fertile, so they are ideal for crops of all kinds and agriculture is a major occupation. (2) Thousands of years ago the first civilisations developed around rivers in fertile plains, and a large part of the world's population still lives in plains. (3) About 40 crore people, more than one-fourth of India's population, live in the Ganga plain. (4) Their gentle slope makes river navigation easy, which supports a lot of economic activity and travel. (5) Problems: irrigation has contributed to the depletion of groundwater, a challenge for the future of farming, and the Ganga plains also suffer from high population and pollution. So plains attract people but bring their own challenges.
s: Fertile sediment soil makes plains ideal for crops
First civilisations grew in river plains, and many people still live in plains
Ganga plain: about 40 crore people, more than one-fourth of India
Easy river navigation on the gentle slope supports economic activity
Problems: groundwater depletion from irrigation, high population, pollution

questions.q: Which of these does the chapter give as an example of a cold desert?
questions.a: The Gobi Desert in Asia
o: The Thar Desert in the Indian Subcontinent

questions.q: In the table of the five tinais of ancient Tamil Sangam poetry, which landscape and main occupation go with Mullai?
questions.a: Grassland and forests, with cattle rearing
o: Grassland and forests, with cattle rearing
Mountainous regions, with hunting and gathering
Coastal regions, with fishing and seafaring

questions.q: The chapter describes four landforms: mountains, plateaus, plains and deserts. Which of these tinais has a landscape that matches none of the four?
questions.a: Neydal

questions.q: An old Sanskrit poem describes a wind from the Himalaya 'cooling the mountain people after they hunt deer'. Which tinai links its landscape with the kind of work these people do?
questions.a: Kurinji

questions.q:
Match each tinai in Column A with its main occupation in Column B.
Column A: 1. Kurinji  2. Marudam  3. Neydal  4. Palai
Column B: A. journeying and fighting  B. hunting and gathering  C. fishing and seafaring  D. farming
State True or False, and give a reason: 'Deserts are one of the three main landforms described in the chapter.'

s: States the verdict: False

questions.q: (a) What does the chapter mean by 'resilience'? (b) Using the chapter's account of the Thar Desert, give one example of human resilience.
questions.a: (a) Resilience is the capacity to meet challenges and difficulties, adapt to them or overcome them. (b) Despite harsh living conditions, communities live in the Thar Desert or migrate through it, and they hold rich cultural traditions such as folk songs and legends related to the desert.
s: Defines resilience as the capacity to meet, adapt to or overcome challenges
Gives the Thar example: people live in or migrate through the desert despite harsh conditions and keep rich traditions

questions.q: (a) How many landscapes do the tinais name, and how many main landforms does the chapter describe? (b) Which tinai matches the chapter's plains, and does its occupation agree with what the chapter says about the Ganga plain? (c) What do the tinais show about the link between people and the natural environment?
questions.a: (a) The tinais name five landscapes; the chapter describes three main landforms (mountains, plateaus and plains). (b) Marudam, the fertile agricultural plains, linked with farming; this agrees with the chapter, which says agriculture is a major occupation in the Ganga plain. (c) They show a keen awareness of diverse regions and their characteristics, and a deep connection between humanity and the natural environment.
s: Five tinai landscapes against three main landforms
Marudam with farming, agreeing with agriculture as a major occupation of the Ganga plain
States the deep connection between people and the natural environment, or a keen awareness of regions

questions.q:
A travel company runs three tours. Tour 1 crosses the Sahara Desert in Africa. Tour 2 crosses the Gobi Desert in Asia. Tour 3 visits villages in the Thar Desert, where the evenings are spent listening to folk songs and old legends about the desert. The brochure says every tour goes to places where 'it hardly ever rains or snows'. One customer plans to pack only light cotton clothes for all three tours.
(a) Which of the three tours goes to a cold desert?
(b) Write the brochure's phrase in the chapter's own words for this feature of deserts.
(c) What does the evening programme of Tour 3 show about people in the Thar Desert?
(d) Evaluate the customer's packing plan.
questions.a: (a) Tour 2: the Gobi Desert is a cold desert (the Sahara and the Thar are hot). (b) Deserts are large, dry expanses with very little precipitation. (c) Despite harsh living conditions, people have adapted to the Thar Desert and hold rich cultural traditions, such as folk songs and legends, related to it. (d) The plan suits the hot deserts, the Sahara and the Thar, but not the Gobi, which is cold; she should pack warm clothes for Tour 2. Very little rain does not mean a desert is hot.
s: (a) Tour 2, the Gobi, a cold desert
(b) Large, dry expanses with very little precipitation
(c) People have adapted to the desert and keep rich traditions such as folk songs and legends
(d) Light clothes suit the hot Sahara and Thar but not the cold Gobi

questions.q: The tinai table links each landscape with a main occupation. Check how well three tinais match what the rest of the chapter says about the same kind of land. (a) Kurinji (mountainous regions): compare its occupation with the ways of earning the chapter describes for mountain people. (b) Marudam (fertile agricultural plains): compare it with the chapter's account of the Ganga plain. (c) Palai (arid, desert-like regions): compare it with what the chapter says about people of the Thar Desert. (d) Using (a) to (c), say whether the tinais and the chapter agree that landscape shapes work, and where they differ.
questions.a: (a) Kurinji is linked with hunting and gathering, while the chapter's mountain people practise terrace farming, herding (often preferred over agriculture) and tourism: both tie work to mountain land, but the occupations named differ. (b) Marudam is linked with farming, and the chapter says agriculture is a major occupation of the Ganga plain (along with river fishing): a close match. (c) Palai is linked with journeying and fighting; the chapter says communities live in the Thar or migrate through it, so journeying partly fits, but the chapter says nothing of fighting. (d) Both agree that the kind of land shapes the work people do; they differ in the details because the tinais are a different, older classification from ancient Tamil poetry, while the chapter describes how people live in these landforms.
s: (a) Kurinji's hunting and gathering against terrace farming, herding and tourism: partly differ
(b) Marudam's farming matches agriculture in the Ganga plain
(c) Palai's journeying partly fits people migrating through the Thar; fighting is not in the chapter
(d) Both link landscape to work; details differ because the tinais are an older, different classification
